method.label: Bound the excess by geometric sequences

annotationRationale: The shifted recurrence yields geometric upper and lower bounds by induction and repeated multiplication. A positive-term binomial expansion supplies the upper endpoint estimate.
sourceMethod: Followed the official substitution y_n=x_n-4 and comparison with geometric sequences of ratios 9/10 and 10/11. Made positivity explicit and applied the official power estimates directly at indices 80 and 200.

review.mathCheck: The substitution gives \(y_{n+1}=y_n(y_n+9)/(y_n+10)\) with \(0<y_n\le1\), so \((9/10)^n<y_n\le(10/11)^n\). Since \((9/10)^4>1/2\) and \((11/10)^{10}>2\), we obtain \(y_{80}>2^{-20}\) and \(y_{200}<2^{-20}\). Thus m exists and \(81\le m\le200\), entirely within choice C.
review.sourceMethodCheck: The explanation faithfully adapts official solution 24 on pages 12–13 with original prose. It uses the same shift, geometric comparisons and positive-term expansion, expressing the endpoint argument directly at indices 80 and 200. Its strict lower bound is valid.
review.annotationCheck: The recurrence, geometric comparison and base-and-step argument support the assessed nodes. Binomial expansion appropriately supports the upper estimate; its needed terms and positivity are explained. Rational-expression simplification and inequality manipulation are background.

The solution does not assess every criterion of these broader topics, such as recovering a common ratio or finding an arbitrary binomial coefficient.
